newsitem.title: POLAND: POLES BAFFLED, SCEPTICAL OVER CONSTITUTION VOTE.
newsitem.headline: POLES BAFFLED, SCEPTICAL OVER CONSTITUTION VOTE.

text.p: Poles vote in a referendum on Sunday on whether they approve a hotly-debated new constitution drafted by parliament to enshrine democracy -- but an opinion poll shows that most have little idea what it says.

"A month before the constitutional referendum, only nine percent of respondents judged that they had good knowledge of the fundamental law," public polling organisation CBOS said in a report published on Tuesday.

"The largest section of those polled (43 percent) admitted they were poorly informed and a further 27 percent knew absolutely nothing on the subject," CBOS said after the April 11-15 poll of a representative random sample of 1,201 adults.
Public debate has raged for months around the constitution, designed to replace a 1952 one made obsolete by the 1989 fall of communism and by interim arrangements passed in the 199Os.

The version drafted by parliament, a compromise between the two ruling parties rooted in the communist era and two opposition groups, is opposed by rightists grouped around the Solidarity union who want Poles to reject it.

Some analysts view the referendum as a test of strength before general elections due in September when the Solidarity Election Action (AWS) and other rightists, now underrepresented in parliament, hope to supplant the ruling ex-communists.

The law prevents surveys predicting the outcome so soon before the vote but the last CBOS poll, in March, suggested 41 percent of those tooking part would vote for the constitution, 15 percent would reject it and the rest were undecided.
The widespread ignorance of the issues comes despite intensive broadcast debates and other publicity.
The ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski has sent the 243-section document to all households with an appeal for support, despite charges that this is unwarranted meddling.

The right's objections to the constitution centre on charges that it fails to reflect the historic ties between Poland and the Roman Catholic Church, to which 90 percent of Poles belong, at least formally.

The bishops have announced strong moral reservations over the constitution, notably its lack of a clause effectively banning abortion -- which has recently been liberalised by the ex-communists and other secular-minded parliamentarians.
Although there is no minimum turnout required to make the vote valid, politicians are appealing for large participation.
But the latest CBOS (Centre for Public Opinion Research) survey reads ominously for such hopes.

It found that more than half of all Poles thought the constitution was unlikely to strengthen democracy, lead to better government or lessen the sharp polarisation in politics. -- Anthony Barker +48 22 653 9700
